items.title: Jerry Dodgion interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996
items.q: I know I read about one fellow who did a very extensive study on Sonny Rollins

ctx.x: That’s hard you know because I never did really study how to play jazz. Like they have colleges that you can go to now and you can major in jazz. You can learn in three weeks now what took me fifteen years to learn. But I know it’s information-wise, you know? So it’s really hard, and I’m not a teacher either, I don’t do any teaching. So it’s hard for me to tell somebody how I feel about what I’m doing, it really is. So maybe if I were better at that I would have been a teacher. I don’t know.

Yeah. Well sometimes your own style is the hardest to talk about. I know I read about one fellow who did a very extensive study on Sonny Rollins and how he apparently developed all these motifs and after Sonny Rollins read it then he felt he couldn’t do it anymore, because now he was thinking too hard about it. Where before it was just a natural thing. Now that someone tells him what he’s doing, it’s hard to do now.

That’s possible. Because when you’re doing it, or when I’m doing it anyway, I’m not thinking of how I’m doing it. You just try to play your best and to fit in with what’s happening around you. That’s the main thing for me. I mean if I play with sensitive players it’s very easy to play and you don’t get tired, you have a lot of fun. And if you play with people that aren’t sensitive, that aren’t listening to each other and stuff, pretty soon you find, I’m really getting tired and the music is not fun, what am I…
